title: The Knight, the Princess and the Sun-Dragon
author: TravellerMTL
tags: dragon, knight, princess, rescue, short novel, completed
description:
Princess Meera of Kesaripur has been carried off to the Burning Peak by SuarJ, a golden dragon who glows like the noon sun and hoards everything that shines.

Sir Arjun, the least decorated knight in the kingdom, rides out to save her with a borrowed horse, a dented shield and a very bad map. But when he finally reaches the mountain, he discovers the princess has been making plans of her own.

A short, complete fantasy adventure in six chapters.

chapters.title: The Day the Sun Came Down
chapters.text:
On the morning of the harvest festival, the sun rose twice over Kesaripur.

The first sunrise was the ordinary kind, pink and gentle over the mustard fields. The second came an hour later, from the west, and it had wings.

It was a dragon, gold from snout to tail, so bright that the palace guards had to squint up at it through their fingers. Its scales threw light across the marketplace like a thousand polished coins. Where its shadow passed, the air grew warm enough to ripen every mango in the royal orchard at once.

"SuarJ," whispered the old gardener, dropping his rake. "The sun-dragon of the Burning Peak. I thought he was a story."

The dragon circled the palace three times. Then he landed on the highest balcony, where Princess Meera had been standing with a cup of tea, trying to decide whether the festival speech needed more jokes.

"You shine," SuarJ said to her, in a voice like a furnace door swinging open.

"I beg your pardon?"

"Your crown. Your bangles. Your eyes, a little. I collect things that shine." He tilted his great golden head. "You're coming with me."

Before a single guard could draw a sword, the dragon closed his claws gently around the princess, balcony railing and all, and leapt into the sky.

The tea cup fell. It was the only thing in the kingdom that moved for a full ten seconds.

Then everyone began to scream at once.

chapters.title: The Least Decorated Knight
chapters.text:
The king called for his bravest knights.

Sir Vikram had a sprained ankle. Sir Dev was at his cousin's wedding in the next kingdom. Sir Rohan, the bravest of all, took one look at the smoking outline of the balcony and discovered an urgent need to inspect the southern border.

That left Sir Arjun.

Sir Arjun had been a knight for exactly eleven days. He had no medals, no famous victories, and no horse of his own. His armour had belonged to his uncle, who had been considerably shorter, so his ankles showed when he walked.

"You," said the king, without much hope. "Can you rescue my daughter?"

Arjun thought about it honestly, because that was the kind of person he was.

"I don't know, Your Majesty," he said. "But I'm the one who's here, so I think I should try."

The king blinked. It was, he realised, the first sensible thing anyone had said all morning.

By noon Arjun was riding out of the city gate on a borrowed horse named Biscuit, with a dented shield, a sword that needed sharpening, a bag of samosas from the palace kitchen, and a map of the Burning Peak drawn by someone who had clearly never been there. Half of it was labelled "PROBABLY MOUNTAINS".

Behind him, the whole city lined the walls to watch him go. Nobody cheered. They were all too busy trying to remember his name.

chapters.title: Riddles at the River of Glass
chapters.text:
The road to the Burning Peak ran through three days of forest and ended at a river that looked like molten glass. It was so hot it shimmered, and no boat could cross it.

On the far bank sat a small grey heron, the guardian of the crossing.

"Answer my riddle and I will show you the stepping stones," said the heron. "Answer wrongly and you go home."

"All right," said Arjun, climbing off Biscuit.

"What grows bigger the more you take from it?"

Arjun frowned. He was not good at riddles. He thought about bread, and debts, and his uncle's temper, none of which seemed right.

Biscuit, who was bored, began digging at the riverbank with one hoof. The hole grew wider. And wider.

"A hole!" Arjun said. "The more you take away, the bigger it gets."

The heron looked faintly disappointed, the way guardians always do when someone gets it right. With a flick of its beak it tapped the water, and a line of flat black stones rose to the surface, cool enough to walk on.

Halfway across, Arjun stopped and offered the heron a samosa.

"Why?" asked the heron, suspicious.

"You must get hungry, guarding a river all day."

The heron ate the samosa in one gulp. Then, after a long pause, it said, "The dragon sleeps from noon until the second bell. Everything he loves, he keeps in the east cavern. Good luck, small knight."

It was, Arjun later learned, the first time the heron had ever given anyone advice.

chapters.title: The Princess Has a Plan
chapters.text:
Princess Meera had not spent her captivity waiting to be rescued.

On the first day she had explored the dragon's lair: a vast cavern at the top of the Burning Peak, heaped with everything that shone. Golden plates. Brass lamps. Mirrors, spoons, temple bells, a thousand polished coins, and one very confused peacock.

On the second day she had noticed that the dragon, for all his terrifying brightness, was lonely.

On the third day she had started talking to him.

"Why do you collect all this?" she asked, as SuarJ arranged a row of silver bowls by size.

The dragon was quiet for a long time. "When I was young," he said at last, "there were other sun-dragons. The sky was full of us. Then, one by one, they flew away to wherever old dragons go, and the sky became very dark. So I gather things that shine. It makes the cave feel less empty."

Meera looked at the heaps of treasure, glittering in the dragon's glow, and felt something she had not expected to feel. Sympathy.

"SuarJ," she said carefully, "things that shine don't keep you company. People do."

"People run away from me."

"Some of them might not," said the princess, "if you stopped kidnapping them."

The dragon considered this with the slow seriousness of a creature that has lived four hundred years.

That was when a small knight with visible ankles climbed over the edge of the cave, holding a dented shield in front of him, and shouted, "Release the princess, foul beast!"

Meera put her face in her hands.

"Oh no," she said. "Not now."

chapters.title: A Duel That Nobody Wins
chapters.text:
SuarJ rose to his full height. The cavern filled with light so fierce that Arjun's shield grew warm in his hands.

"You dare," the dragon rumbled, "enter the Burning Peak?"

"I do," said Arjun. His voice shook, but he did not step back. "I've come for Princess Meera."

"Arjun, wait," said the princess. "It isn't what it looks like."

"It looks like a dragon kidnapped you."

"All right, it's a little bit what it looks like."

The dragon breathed out a warning plume of golden fire over the knight's head. It singed the plume off his helmet. Arjun lifted his blunt sword anyway and charged.

It was, by any fair measure, the least impressive duel in the history of Kesaripur. Arjun's sword bounced off the dragon's scales with a sound like a spoon hitting a pot. SuarJ swatted him gently with one wing and sent him tumbling into a pile of brass lamps. Arjun got up. SuarJ swatted him again. Arjun got up again.

On the seventh time, the dragon stopped.

"Why do you keep standing up?" SuarJ asked, genuinely puzzled. "You cannot win."

Arjun wiped soot from his face. "Because she's still here," he said. "And nobody else came."

The cavern went very quiet.

SuarJ looked at the battered knight, and then at the princess, and then at his enormous, glittering, empty collection.

"Nobody has ever come back for anything I took," the dragon said softly. "Not once, in four hundred years."

chapters.title: The Sun Comes Home
chapters.text:
In the end, it was the princess who wrote the treaty, on the back of Arjun's terrible map.

SuarJ would return every stolen bell to its temple and every golden plate to its kitchen. In exchange, the people of Kesaripur would hold a new festival every year on the harvest morning: the Festival of Two Suns. On that day every lamp, mirror and polished pot in the kingdom would be carried up to the city walls to shine toward the Burning Peak.

"So I'll know I'm not alone," SuarJ said, reading it over with one enormous golden eye.

"So everyone will know you're not a story," Meera corrected.

They flew home together, the princess riding on the dragon's neck, the knight clinging nervously to a spike near the tail, and Biscuit the horse dangling from SuarJ's claws, complaining the entire way.

When the city saw the sun-dragon coming, the walls filled with screaming. Then they saw the princess waving, and the screaming turned into the loudest cheer Kesaripur had ever heard.

The king offered Sir Arjun a medal, a castle, and his daughter's hand in marriage.

Arjun accepted the medal, politely declined the castle, and said the last part was entirely up to the princess.

Meera laughed, took his sooty hand, and said she would think about it over tea, which she finally got to drink.

And every harvest morning after that, the sun rose twice over Kesaripur: once in the east, pink and gentle, and once from the west, golden and glad, circling the city three times before landing in the square to be greeted by a thousand shining mirrors and one small, grinning knight.

*The End.*
